A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViF research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original attention analyses, token-dropping experiments, benchmark evaluations and ablations in Sections 2 and 4 and Appendices B and D.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds multi-image/video evaluations, alternative-relay comparisons, robustness tests and efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: Unimodal token selection, instruction contextualization, attention reallocation, the Key-Norm alternative and two-stage training are retained. Expanded mask and MAS descriptions document the existing procedure; the new relay alternatives are comparison experiments rather than changes to ViF.

E1.justification: V3 extends the original eight benchmarks to multi-image understanding with MMIU and MuirBench and video understanding with MVBench and Video-MME (Table 4). Appendix D.2 also introduces masked and mismatched-image scenarios, substantially broadening evaluated input conditions.

E2.justification: The original MemVR, VISTA, FarSight, DeCo and TAME comparisons remain. V3 Table 11 adds pooling, MLP and transformer compression and SAM2-based object-level relays as substantive alternatives. Figure 11 additionally compares combinations of ViF with the five existing mitigators against standalone methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include injecting corrupted images at turns 2–4 and evaluating subsequent recovery, measuring latency and FLOPs, bilinearly downsampling CHAIR images, checking another hallucination judge, and inspecting three-turn linear trajectories. The existing training settings and original benchmark metrics are retained; these additions do not establish reruns of earlier experiments.

E4.justification: V3 adds tests of relay representation and token mixtures, corrupted-input recovery, compatibility with other mitigators, judge sensitivity, efficiency scaling and generated-answer case studies (Tables 8, 11 and 15; Figures 10–12). The original component ablations and hyperparameter sweeps remain and should not be counted as new.

E5.justification: No repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are added or revised. The new cross-judge discrepancy result is a sensitivity analysis, rather than uncertainty estimation for the reported benchmark scores.

E6.justification: Original table values are retained, but substantial new benchmark, efficiency, robustness and combination results appear. For example, new Table 4 reports LLaVA-NeXT-7B MMIU scores of 31.6 without ViF and 33.9 with it. Figure 11 also reports a negative combination result: VISTA falls from 91.2 alone to 87.9 with ViF. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under matched conditions.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7, including attention allocation, reallocation and the hallucination snowballing score, retain their mathematical content. No new theorem, proof or formal assumption is introduced; the additional mask explanation clarifies existing operations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the same central claims about hallucination propagation, declining visual attention and mitigation through unimodal visual relays. Replacing 'plug-and-play' with 'model-agnostic' does not otherwise redefine the scientific contribution.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations concerning compression loss, recovery through renewed visual grounding and the source of computational overhead. It also calls for better combinations with other mitigators and improved token selection. These extend the discussion while retaining the central attention-degradation explanation and existing model-coverage limitations.

D1.justification: V3 identifies GPT-5-20250807 as the HS judge and supplies its complete scoring prompt, addressing a consequential omission in v1. Appendix C.1 expands the actor/critic collaboration description, and the abstract reports code as publicly available rather than forthcoming. These are documentation and access-statement changes; the training recipe and hardware disclosure are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds references for the new benchmarks, Gemini, a MAS survey and object-level visual processing, among other bibliography additions. Appendix A and the central positioning against single-agent hallucination mitigation remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. V3 expands the MAS explanation into Appendix C.1, moves limitations into the conclusion, reorders additional analyses, abbreviates OneVision as OV and revises terminology and cross-references. This is limited reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: V3 adds four tables, three figures and a formatted judge-prompt box, substantially expanding the visual presentation. Existing displays are rearranged and renumbered, sensitivity-table metric arrows are corrected, and the Qwen2.5 layer-attention panel has a revised horizontal range. Most original displays are otherwise reused.

improvement.justification: V1 left the HS judge unspecified and lacked comparisons against compressed/object-level relays and measurements of inference cost. V3 addresses these gaps with judge documentation, direct controls, efficiency measurements and robustness checks, substantially strengthening reproducibility and evidential support. Broader visual-task evaluations further support applicability. Minor reporting overstatements remain, including the under-3% 34B FLOPs-overhead claim despite Table 8 reaching about 3.3%.
